content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors investigate why Vision-Transformer (ViT) based models (e.g. vanilla ViT or Swin) are more robust to adversarial attacks while being underconfident in their predictions. Through a variety of experiments they conclude that this is because the error landscape for ViT-based models has a curvature not observed on CNN-based models, which makes FGSM based attacks more difficult.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
* Interesting and thorough experimental analysis
* Might have an impact on how we use adversarial attacks on ViT based models
* Might give a direction on how to improve training of ViT based models.

Weaknesses
* Unclear if this finding is due to actual model differences or differences in the optimization. The authors state in the appendix that they follow the default training procedure of the original publication when training a Swin Transformer model. So it stands to reason that they did the same for the other models, or that they used freely available downloadable models. If that is the case, it is likely that the models were trained with different optimizers and augmentations. As such, it is unclear if this the findings they report are truly due to differences of ViT versus CNN, or something else. For example, I could imagine that using Mixup or Cutmix would severely affect how the loss landscape looks around single datapoints. Same goes for certain optimization and regularization techniques. Unless all models underwent the same training procedure, it is a moot point to argue that observed differences are due to model differences, since there are too many other possible explanations. The authors must make sure that all models were trained the same way.

* No investigations into where this curvature comes from: While the authors explore when high-curvature points emerge, they do not investigate how they are formed. Is there something that distinguishes high-curvature points visually from their counterparts? Does the high loss cause curvature, or the curvature cause high loss? Are all classes affected equally? I understand that there is only so much space to cover experiments in a single paper, but this paper raises more questions than it answers.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* As pointed out above, the authors did not give enough information about the models they investigated: were they trained on the same data set, with the same data augmentation techniques and optimizers?

* I was able to easily follow along the paper, it is well written

* ‘how the output feature of the penultimate layer (which is simply referred to as output in this paper)” => Which layer is this exactly? Do you count the classification head / linear layer as “ultimate” layer, or is this the previous-to-last dense layer in the last MLP of a transformer block?  Is this before or after applying Global Average Pooling? Do you se CLS tokens for ViT, and if so, do you look at the whole representation or just the CLS token?

* Figure 11: plotting absolute change might drive the point home even clearer. Having green as baseline intermixed with green&blue is not a good choice of palette.

* Section 5: I can’t follow this section, mostly because I lack a crucial piece of information: the authors claim that “certain training data seem to be trapped in curved regions, which obstructs the training of the network.”.  That would only be the case if these datapoints are trapped in these regions WHILE STILL HAVING A HIGH LOSS.  However, I see no convincing evidence that high-curvature points (high \theta^{(1)}) are stuck at significantly larger loss values than low-curvature ones. It _could_ be somewhat visible in Figure 12, but the figure is too small to make it out, plus overlapping dots make it hard to estimate densities. I’d appreciate if the authors could make this point clearer.

* Some minor style points:  "(and we show that Transformers are actually underconfident in this paper)"  => there is a full sentence in a parenthesis here!  “The high robustness, however, does not comport with underconfidence.” => “comport” is not the right verb in this sentence
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors perform an analysis of the loss landscape near training datapoints of ViT based models and CNNs. Due to oversights in the experimental design it is unclear if the conclusions drawn by the authors do actually hold.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this work, an empirical justification is presented on why transformers are under-confidant while robust to advarsarial perturbation. It has been shown experimentally that while traversing linearly along the adversarial perturbation in the input space, the feature space moves along a curved space. Instead of advarsarial perturbation, if a random purturbation is given in the first iteration, then the feature space moves linearly. The gradient direction moves in the early iterations for the points in curved space and hence large distance from the decision boundary. Although transformers are under confidant, but it has large decision boundaries in the curved space.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths 
 * A lot of experiments were carried out to demonstrate robustness, confidence in model prediction, difficulty in training, and distance from the decision boundary of Transformers over CNN. 
* A number of questions were addressed empirically, for example, why Transformers are robust while underconfident? 

Weaknesses
* No theoretical justification is given on why the curved space is created by the Transformers not CNNs 
* Most of the questions answered here are experimental and observational. 
* Different notations are being used throughout the draft - r + FGSM; rFGSM (Fig. 4.b); rFGSM + FGSM (Fig 4.a); rand + FGSM (Fig 5.h)
* Passage to the decision boundary is computed in eq-3 with the adversarial direction in eq-4. Instead of adversarial attack, one can employ any other types of attacks, eg, random attack, it will be interesting to see if the feature space will still be in the random direction even after random attacks.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-written and results are clearly presented. Novelty is limited as no theoretical insight has been demonstrated. The work is certainly reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work might lead to better understanding of vision transformers, however, all the results and evidence are empirical that makes transformers still very mysterious. It is still unknown what promotes curved features space in transformers compared to CNNs.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper starts from the counter-intuitive phenomenon that Transformers are more robust than CNNs but their predictions are under-confident.

Then the author first quantitatively demonstrated this phenomenon by a) proposing and measuring the signed ECE and b) measuring the traveled distance that makes a sample across the decision boundary and misclassified.

The authors visualized in feature space in 2D and observe that the linear input space around an input sample is curved in the feature space while it is more linear in the CNN feature space. They also verified the assumption empirically by showing the travel distance is larger and the direction at each step changes more in Transformers' feature spaces than CNNs'. 

This curved region around a sample potentially contributes to the robustness of Transformers to the noise from the input space, but once the sample jumps out of the region it is still vulnerable to adversarial attack. The curved regions are also observed at the early stage when training a transformer, which makes the loss difficult to be minimized if a sample is located in the curved region. All these observations indicate opportunities for future research such as reducing the negative impact of these curved regions during training.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
+ The paper is well motivated and organized, where the authors start from the counter-intuitive phenomenon of better robustness but under-confidence and then observe the curved region when investigating why the travel distance of a sample is larger in a Transformer than a CNN.
+ The experiments are well-designed and intuitive, which makes it easier for the audience to understand the observations and the corresponding insights.

Weakness:
+ The paper have great observations but it would be better if the authors can demonstrate some simple use cases of the observations (which are all left for future research currently).
+ A deeper analysis would be helpful:
    + The author mainly compares Swin with Resnet, which both utilize the locality of the image structure. But how the curved region differs btween vanilla ViT and Swin?
    + Besides the comparison between network architectures, analysis of data samples would also be helpful, i.e. what kind of data samples are within the curved region, and how strong the curvature is.
+ The paper can be more self-contained, for example, what is the definition of confidence here? I think it means the predicted probabilities after softmax (correct me if I misunderstand), but there is no definition in the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper is well-organized and generally clearly written. 
It utilizes some existing tools but the observations are novel to the best of my knowledge.
It is also easy to reproduce since most of the necessary components are standard and off-the-shelf.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper has inspiring observations with sufficient insights. The curved region potentially can be utilized either in designing better architecture or optimizer. 
But some deeper analysis or simple use cases would be helpful. 
So I lean to accept the paper and will adjust my rating based on the authors' response.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper studied the working principle of Vision Transformers from the perspective of the input-output relationship. As found in the paper that for certain data, Transformers move the output along a nonlinear trajectory within a certain range which leads to better robustness for Transformers, whereas CNNs show fairly linear movements of the output.

This paper studied and replied to the following questions: a) How does the representation space of Transformers look like? b) What makes Transformers robust to input perturbation? c) Then, why is the prediction of Transformers underconfident? d) When are the curved regions created and how do they influence the training process? 

Overall, this work is exciting and vital. But it has not been studied in depth, and some experiments are relatively simple.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1) This is an interesting and important research direction. With the development of deep learning, security issues are unavoidable, and it is undoubtedly helpful to better understand how the model works.
2) The figures in the paper are intuitive and easy to interpret.

Weaknesses:
1) The questions and studies are great, but not deep enough, and many parts of the experiments are relatively simple.
2) The full paper is based on the observational phenomenon for analysis, which may lack some theoretical support.
3) Some of the content is confusing. Please refer ‘Clarity, Quality, Novelty And Reproducibility’ for details.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Some comments and questions:
1) Is there a limitation to having only the penultimate layer of analysis? Different layers have different functions in the network. Can we further show the change process of the representation of different layers to explain the representation space of Transformers better?
2) On page 2, there are: 'for some input data, the directions of successive movements of the output significantly change in the case of Transformers unlike CNNs'. Is 'some input data' random? Or is there some characteristic that causes this phenomenon in Transformers?
3) Why does add randomness help the data to jump out of the curved region? In other words: Why can the random directions escape the curved region? Instead, the direction determined by the attack perturbation will wander in the curved region.
4) Some models that are more difficult to compute gradients may have better robustness to FGSM. How to determine whether the robustness is related to the curved region?
5) Maybe can use Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) instead of I-FGSM. PGD is a more powerful attack with a similar pattern to I-FGSM.
6) Although the paper answers when the curved region is generated, I am more curious about why the curved region is generated. Is there any inference? 
7) Should the blue curve be used to represent z(0) to z(1) in Figure 4. (b)? My understanding is that the movement inside the curved region will follow the direction of the curve, so for the same length of distance, the straight distance inside is smaller than the outside, resulting in data cannot escape the curved region.

The research direction in this paper is exciting and vital. But it has not been studied in depth, and some experiments are relatively simple.

content.title: Curved Representation Space of Vision Transformers
content.abstract: Neural networks with self-attention (a.k.a. Transformers) like ViT and Swin have emerged as a better alternative to traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for computer vision tasks. However, our understanding of how the new architecture works is still limited. In this paper, we focus on the phenomenon that Transformers show higher robustness against corruptions than CNNs, while not being overconfident (in fact, we find Transformers are actually underconfident). This is contrary to the intuition that robustness increases with confidence. We resolve this contradiction by investigating how the output of the penultimate layer moves in the representation space as the input data moves within a small area. In particular, we show the following. (1) While CNNs exhibit fairly linear relationship between the input and output movements, Transformers show nonlinear relationship for some data. For those data, the output of Transformers moves in a curved trajectory as the input moves linearly. (2) When a data is located in a curved region, it is hard to move it out of the decision region since the output moves along a curved trajectory instead of a straight line to the decision boundary, resulting in high robustness of Transformers. (3) If a data is slightly modified to jump out of the curved region, the movements afterwards become linear and the output goes to the decision boundary directly. Thus, Transformers can be attacked easily after a small random jump and the perturbation in the final attacked data remains imperceptible. In other words, there does exist a decision boundary near the data, which is hard to find only because of the curved representation space. This also explains the underconfident prediction of Transformers. (4) The curved regions in the representation space start to form at an early training stage and grow throughout the training course. Some data are trapped in the regions, obstructing Transformers from reducing the training loss.
